parsed.study_design: Descriptive cross-sectional mixed-method study, primarily quantitative
parsed.population_and_sample: Inmates and selected staff at a maximum-security correctional facility in Southwest Nigeria; 396 consenting inmates from 420 randomly selected, plus staff key informants and facility observations.
parsed.exposure: Institutional and administrative conditions governing prison WASH provision, including toilet type and number, water availability, prison-supplied hygiene materials, maintenance and cleaning arrangements, overcrowding, and nighttime toilet access.
parsed.outcome: Sanitation-service access and exclusion measures, including continuous and nighttime toilet access, queuing and waiting time, toilet availability and overflow, water scarcity, toilet-cleaning frequency, and handwashing access and practices.
parsed.rationale: The Methods identify a descriptive cross-sectional mixed-method design using inmate interviews, staff interviews, facility observations, and administrative health records (pp. 2201–2204). The Results report direct sanitation-access outcomes—only 57.6% always had toilet access, inmates commonly queued, and some had no in-cell toilet—alongside institutional determinants such as water availability, toilet type and number, cleaning schedules, and prison provision of soap (pp. 2204–2211). These constitute empirical evidence on how correctional-facility governance and administration shape access to sanitation and hygiene services.
